altitude.note: Ice-surface elevation given by NSF for the station; the array is beneath the same ice surface.
altitude.quote: Positioned at 90°S, the geographic South Pole. Sits atop the Antarctic ice sheet at an elevation of approximately 2,835 meters (9,301 feet) above sea level.

coordinates.locator: IceCube — Detector, opening paragraph; NSF station page, “Location”
coordinates.note: No official IceCube or NSF page publishes the latitude/longitude of the array. The array sits in the ice next to the station at the geographic South Pole, so the pole itself (90°S) is recorded with precision_m = 2000, which covers the ~1 km array footprint and its offset from the pole marker. Longitude is degenerate at the pole and is recorded as 0. Do not treat this as a surveyed position.
coordinates.quote: IceCube, the South Pole neutrino observatory, is a cubic-kilometer particle detector made of Antarctic ice and located near the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station.

depth.note: Depth range of the instrumented part of the in-ice array below the ice surface.
depth.quote: The DOMs are attached to vertical “strings,” frozen into 86 boreholes and arrayed over a cubic kilometer from 1,450 meters to 2,450 meters depth.

name: South Pole — IceCube array
notes: The ice sheet, and with it the whole array, drifts about 10 m per year (NSF: “Due to ice movement, the station drifts approximately 10 meters (33 feet) each year.”), so any fixed coordinate is only meaningful at ~10 m/yr precision anyway.

The IceCube detector paper (arXiv:1612.05093) states that IceCube is located at Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station but publishes no geographic coordinates; the IceCube internal coordinate system is a local grid (eastings/northings), not lat/lon.

summary.plain: The patch of Antarctic ice next to the South Pole station where a cubic kilometre of sensors is frozen in, between about 1.5 and 2.5 kilometres below the surface.
summary.technical: Ice-embedded detector site at the geographic South Pole; 86 boreholes on a 125 m hexagonal grid instrumented between 1,450 m and 2,450 m depth, with the IceTop surface array above and the IceCube Laboratory at the surface.
